content.title: Route Handlers: When the App Exposes an HTTP Boundary
content.hook: Sometimes a Next.js application needs to expose an HTTP endpoint.
content.context:
The App Router provides Route Handlers.

A simplified route can look like:

```text
app/
  api/
    products/
      route.ts
```

That file can define how the application responds to HTTP requests.

activities.title: Why is this different from a page?

content.title: Why is this different from a page?
content.text:
A page produces UI.

A Route Handler produces an HTTP response.

That makes the mental model:

**Page → interface**

**Route Handler → HTTP boundary**

content.question: Which request belongs in a Route Handler?

options.text: “Respond with product data for an HTTP client.”

feedback.correct: Correct answer: B. “Respond with product data for an HTTP client.”
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: B. “Respond with product data for an HTTP client.”

content.title: Keep responsibilities clear
content.text:
If a page needs product data, that does not automatically mean the browser must call your own Route Handler.

Server-side application code can often access the data directly.

A Route Handler becomes useful when you actually need an HTTP boundary.
